holidays.name: Opposite Day
holidays.description: Today you say the reverse of what you mean, wear your shirt backward, and eat dessert before dinner. Nothing is quite as it seems, and you can claim that today is not Opposite Day.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance with playground roots. It has no known founder, and the idea has spread through schoolyards and pop culture for generations.
holidays.funFact: Opposite Day has a built-in logic puzzle. If someone says it isn't Opposite Day, you can't tell whether they mean it, because on Opposite Day a statement means its reverse.

holidays.name: National Irish Coffee Day
holidays.description: Raise a warm mug of coffee, Irish whiskey, and sugar, topped with a cloud of lightly whipped cream. It's a cozy drink for a cold January day.
holidays.origin: The drink is usually credited to Joe Sheridan, a chef at Foynes airport in Ireland in the 1940s. He is said to have made it to warm up chilly travelers. This day is an unofficial observance, and the drink also has a day on March 17.
holidays.funFact: Irish coffee is traditionally sipped through the cream rather than stirred in. The cold cream floats on the hot coffee and whiskey.

holidays.name: National Fish Taco Day
holidays.description: This is a day for flaky, crispy, or grilled fish tucked into a warm tortilla. Add slaw, a squeeze of lime, and a drizzle of creamy sauce. It's a good excuse to have taco night with seafood.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. The dish itself is tied to the coastal cuisine of Baja California, Mexico.
holidays.funFact: Many food historians trace the fish taco's popularity to Baja California's coastal fishing towns. From there it spread north to beach towns and menus across the United States.
